problem: The lead says the router makes 'the back button, bookmarks and refresh still work without asking the server for a new page'. Back and forward never ask the server, but a bookmark or a refresh does send a full document request; that is exactly why Section 3 needs the index.html fallback rule. As written the lead contradicts Section 3 and teaches the wrong mental model.
fix: Say: 'so the back and forward buttons work, and a bookmarked or refreshed URL shows the right view. A refresh does send a request for that path, so the server must be told to return index.html (Section 3).'

where: Section 2 body (also Exam traps trap 1 and Quiz Q2)

A student cannot tell which component or tag each sentence is about, and the trap and quiz item are unanswerable.
fix: Write the tags inside using escaped angle brackets, e.g. Nested routes render through <Outlet /> in the parent; use <Link to="/posts"> instead of <a href="/posts">; redirect during render with <Navigate to="/posts" replace />; lazy component inside <Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>.

problem: Q7 asks which Angular directive marks where the matched component appears, and the answer is shown only as '.', so the correct token is missing and the question has no answer.
fix: Answer: <router-outlet></router-outlet> (the RouterOutlet directive), placed in the template where the routed component should appear.

where: Section 2, index route and layout route sentences
problem: 'The Route with no path inside a parent is an index route' is not accurate: a Route with no path and no index is a pathless layout route, and an index route is declared with the index prop. The next sentence, 'A layout route has no path of its own except as a wrapper', is also unclear, since layout routes often do carry a path.
fix: Say: a child Route written with index (and no path) is the index route, matched at the parent's URL. A layout route is a parent Route, with or without its own path, whose only job is to keep shared UI such as a header mounted while its children change.
